Title: Anwar surprises diplomats with Bollywood performance [WATCH]
Article:
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim surprised diplomats during his official visit to India for the BRICS Summit by singing a classic Bollywood song.
Anwar, in India for the BRICS Summit, was seen singing the classic Hindi song at a hotel in New Delhi, accompanied by a pianist and with both hands raised in the air.
The song was written by legendary lyricist Majrooh Sultanpuri and sung by Kishore Kumar for the 1965 Bollywood film Teen Deviyan. It was composed by S.D. Burman.
The song explores the wonder and uncertainty of falling in love and is regarded as a classic of Hindi cinema's golden era.
The performance reflected Anwar's long-standing appreciation of Hindi cinema and music, including during his engagements with India, an important economic partner.
The performance was posted on his official X account, formerly Twitter, with the lighthearted caption: "Guru minta izin nyanyi kejap ok!" (Teacher, requesting permission to sing for a bit!).
India Today described the performance as a glimpse into Anwar's long-standing admiration for Hindi cinema and its music, an interest that has also featured in his diplomatic engagements with India.
Anwar is known to be a fan of the late Indian playback legend Lata Mangeshkar, whose distinctive voice made her songs popular across generations.
Her voice became closely associated with Hindi cinema's romantic songs and generations of film music.
It was not his first performance of the song in India. Anwar sang the same number during his 2024 visit to the country.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: One dead, 30 missing after ferry sinks off Vanuatu
Article:
SYDNEY: One person died and 30 are missing after a ferry sank off the coast of Vanuatu, the South Pacific nation's government said on Sunday.
The vessel, MV Matui, had set sail on Friday with more than 40 passengers and crew from the island of Santo to Ambae island in very rough seas, but did not arrive.
"Our hearts and prayers are with the families who have lost loved ones. Search and rescue operations are continuing," read a statement from Vanuatu Prime Minister Jotham Napat's office on Sunday.
Fifteen of those onboard have been "accounted for alive" and one dead body has been recovered, the statement said.
"Over 30 people remain missing at sea," it said.
An investigation into potential negligence has been launched.
"This loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded, and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel," the statement added.
The Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in Noumea, New Caledonia said it is assisting with the search, and a French Armed Forces aircraft was deployed on Sunday morning.
The centre said 12 people were located on Sunday morning.
The member of parliament for Luganville, Matai Seremaiah, who is assisting in the search, said efforts would concentrate on the southeast coast where currents may have carried survivors. — AFP

Title: Houthis claim Saudi base strike as Yemen fighting displaces 76,000
Article:
SANAA: Houthi fighters on Sunday said they used drones and missiles to attack a military base in southern Saudi Arabia as renewed fighting with Yemen's government forces forced growing numbers of civilians to flee.
The attack at the southern Sharurah base targeted "weapons depots and command and control centres that are managing the aggression against our nation and people", Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree wrote on X.
The date of the operation was not specified. Clashes have increased this week between the Iran-allied Houthis and Yemeni government forces, which are backed by Riyadh.
On Saturday, the government forces said they had struck Houthi fighters in the Red Sea city of Mocha, and later attacked other Houthi positions in the southwestern part of the country.
"Air Force of the Armed Forces targeted positions and barracks of the terrorist Houthi group with three airstrikes" in the Taiz region, the Yemeni military said Sunday in a post on X.
US news site Axios also reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman twice called US President Donald Trump to request strikes on the Houthis last week, but that the request was rejected.
The ongoing clashes follow a week-long Houthi offensive that culminated in the group capturing the remainder of Yemen's Red Sea coast and several strategic islands, cementing their hold on the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the sea's southern entrance.
The waterway has become an important artery for Saudi Arabian oil exports after Iran largely cut off shipments through the Gulf with its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the Middle East war.
The Houthis have recently declared their own maritime blockade of Riyadh's Red Sea ports.
The government news agency Saba reported on Saturday that Yemeni "forces destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed members of the Houthi terrorist militia" near the port of Mocha, and quoted a spokesman for the forces as saying they had also struck Houthi targets just outside the city.
The Houthis, meanwhile, said on Saturday evening that over the past 48 hours, "Saudi enemy aircraft conducted 129 airstrikes" on areas under their control.
- 'NOT EVEN A SHELTER' -
Yemen's civil war, which began in 2014 with the Houthi capture of the capital Sanaa, had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022 but roared back to life in July.
Saudi Arabia first entered the war on the side of Yemen's internationally recognised government in 2015 and continues to support the Aden-based administration.
On Saturday night, Saudi authorities said a Houthi projectile fell in an area near the border, hours after issuing alerts warning of the risk of possible attacks.
The civil defence directorate said the incident resulted "in two injuries and material damage to a mosque, several buildings, and vehicles."
The Yemeni civil war has uprooted millions of people, and the latest fighting has led even more to flee their homes.
The fall of Mocha to the Houthis on Thursday drove many residents to Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based.
One of the displaced, Abdulali al-Rajihi, said the Houthis "told us: 'Leave, scatter, you have half an hour'."
"We fled wearing the clothes on our backs. And we took our children, as much as we could manage."
Saddam Ali escaped from Al-Waziyah with his 11 children and a few possessions crammed into a small pick-up truck. He said he hadn't found a single free house in the city, "not even a shelter."
The UN's migration agency said on Saturday that, since July, 76,000 people had fled the fighting, a figure that had quadrupled since last week.
About 1,400 people had fled to Djibouti, the country's minister of economy and finance Ilyas Moussa Dawaleh said on Saturday.
The renewed fighting in Yemen has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides.
- 'FINE AND DANDY' -
Trump on Saturday acknowledged speaking to the de facto Saudi leader but said the Houthis had also "called us and they don't want to fight with us."
He did not elaborate on whether Washington would take any action, but told reporters that "everything's gonna work out fine and dandy" in the region.
In 2025, the United States conducted a seven-week bombing campaign against the Houthis in response to their repeated attacks on Red Sea shipping in support of Hamas in the Gaza war.
That ended with a negotiated ceasefire, though the Houthis kept up their missile and drone attacks targeting Israel.
More recently, the group has resumed attacks on ships in the Red Sea after declaring their maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia.
In Yemen's capital Sanaa, Houthi supporters celebrated the freeing of 210 prisoners held in areas that fell to the group and had spent up to eight years in jail.--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: City folk: Keep walkways clear
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: City dwellers and diners have raised safety and accessibility concerns after Kuala Lumpur City Hall (DBKL) decided to allow restaurant operators to place tables and chairs on walkways.
They said converting pedestrian footpaths into dining areas compromises public safety, obstructs vulnerable groups and prioritises local council revenue over urban mobility.
Hotelier Nizam Hamid, 42, from Jalan Klang Lama, said forcing pedestrians off designated walkways and onto busy roads presents a safety hazard.
"That is the most important safety risk that needs to be evaluated before anything is approved. Food premises must be in a safe and clean environment," he said.
Nizam said walkways have historically served as sheltered pedestrian corridors, providing safe passage alongside shoplots.
"The sidewalk dining also creates physical bottlenecks for foot traffic. This is discriminatory. I believe this decision was made for (eateries) to make money instead of the betterment of the people."
Dentist Dr Sonia A., 35, from Bangsar Baru, said allowing eateries to encroach on footpaths undermines pedestrian safety.
"It is supposed to serve its purpose as a walkway. It feels terribly overcrowded, especially in high foot-traffic areas, which is coincidentally where all eateries are also located."
Dr Sonia, speaking as a parent of a baby girl, said she was concerned about vulnerable pedestrians.
"As a mother of an infant, I think it will be extremely unsafe for my child and myself."
Food and beverage operator Desonny Tuzan said this was a stupid idea — good for businesses, but bad for pedestrians.
"This will cause overcrowding. How can you place tables on a sidewalk right next to a road?"
He added that the disabled will also have a hard time with all the obstructions.
"For sure, it will affect wheelchair users. It is not fair. Parking is already difficult and now people have to manoeuvre wheelchairs over blocked walkways."

Title: Walkway dining welcomed, but safety comes first, say operators
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Restaurant operators have welcomed Kuala Lumpur City Hall's (DBKL) decision to allow eateries to place tables and chairs on five-foot walkways, but emphasised that member restaurants will strictly prioritise customer safety.
Malaysian Indian Restaurant Owners Association president Datuk J. Govindasamy said while operators are eager to start expanding, safety cannot be compromised.
"My advice to members is to apply properly, get the licence and above all, look out for customer safety," he told the New Sunday Times.
"Do not just pay the RM30 fee and put tables in unsafe spots, such as sharp road corners where vehicles turn. Safety must come first."
He said members are awaiting guidelines from DBKL before setting up any outdoor tables.
"I haven't been given any guidelines  yet, but they mentioned we can use the outside space and that guidelines will be sent as soon as possible.
"Once the guidelines are out, we can apply to DBKL and start to operate."
Govindasamy said the initiative will benefit both business owners and local government revenue, provided it is managed safely.
"Most customers prefer sitting outside. It will increase our business while allowing the government to collect revenue through permit fees and taxes."
On concerns about walkways being blocked for pedestrians, wheelchair users and the visually impaired, he said outdoor seating should only be permitted where space allows.
"That is why we have to wait for the guidelines to see which areas DBKL permits. If a five-foot way is narrow, you cannot use it because it will block people. But some walkways are 10 to 12 feet wide, so DBKL will need to establish a proper scale for each location."
He added that they are representing over 200 Indian restaurant operators in Kuala Lumpur.
Malaysian Muslim Restaurant Owners Association Datuk Mohamed Mosin Abdul Razak said while the association supports the move, public accessibility and safety must remain paramount.
"For many restaurants, especially smaller Muslim-owned establishments, the five-foot way provides valuable additional dining space.
"Instead of having a situation where some operators use the space without clear approval while others face enforcement, a proper permit system gives businesses a legal and structured way to operate."
Mosin said pedestrian movement must not be compromised under the new scheme.
"Public access must remain the priority. We support outdoor dining only where there is sufficient space and where pedestrians, wheelchair users, senior citizens, parents with prams and emergency services are not inconvenienced."
While extra seating can boost revenue for smaller venues during peak hours, Mosin urged DBKL to provide clearer guidelines.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: DBKL: Walkway dining policy in place since 2017, subject to conditions
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Allowing eatery operators to place tables and chairs on walkways is not a new policy, but an enhancement of guidelines established in 2017, said Kuala Lumpur City Hall (DBKL).
Responding to queries about public safety concerns and regulatory enforcement, a DBKL spokesman said ongoing improvements to the framework aimed to ensure clearer, standardised implementation aligned with current needs.
"DBKL has not introduced any new policy allowing outdoor tables and chairs. The permit mechanism was already implemented previously.
"What is being done now is an improvement on existing guidelines to ensure execution is clearer, uniform and aligned with current requirements."
DBKL has moved to ease business operations for food premises operators by introducing improvements to streamline services and cut red tape.
It has given approval for operators to put tables and chairs on five-foot walkways with a RM30 monthly permit per table and chair.
The local authority also said outdoor seating approvals are not automatic and restricted to restaurants, eateries and cafes with suitable external space.
On public safety and pedestrian access, the spokesman gave an assurance that both issues remain the top priorities of DBKL when evaluating every application.
"Approvals are subject to  conditions, including ensuring pedestrian walkways remain safe and unobstructed, the location is suitable and that it poses no risk to the public.
"Permit holders are responsible for maintaining safety in the approved areas throughout the permit period."
DBKL added that operators are forbidden from converting public parking bays into dining spaces.
"Parking bays are unauthorised areas for placing tables and chairs because their primary function must be maintained for public parking.
"Converting parking bays will reduce existing parking capacity in high-demand commercial areas, besides posing safety risks to patrons and disrupting traffic flow."
City Hall has conducted 319 operations, seizing 13,173 tables, chairs and other items that were placed illegally outside eateries from January to July this year.
This marked an increase from 286 operations last year, when  6,290 tables, chairs and other items were seized.
City Hall warned that action will be taken against non-compliant premises under By-law 46(1)(d) of the Street, Drainage and Building Act 1974 for placing tables and chairs without a permit or in violation of permit conditions.

Title: [FULL TEXT] Sultan Nazrin's royal address at the 17th SC-OCIS Roundtable
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The following is the royal address by the Sultan of Perak, Sultan Nazrin Muizzuddin Shah, titled "Building Resilience: The Intersection Between Capital, Climate and Innovation". It was delivered at the 17th SC-OCIS Roundtable, held at the Oxford Centre for Islamic Studies in the United Kingdom.
1. Whenever I walk beneath this building's dome, I am reminded that this Centre did not attain its grandeur easily or immediately.
The Oxford Centre for Islamic Studies, which celebrated its 40th anniversary last year, began, as many of you know, in a wooden hut on St Cross Road, funded by a donation that today would not cover the cost of a black cab from the airport. Yet from these humble beginnings back in 1985, a trust was slowly built between scholars from West to East, from Rabat to Mecca to Kuala Lumpur, and a bridge of understanding developed between the intellectual traditions of Oxford and the Muslim world.
2. The beautiful structure around us stands as testament to that vision - a physical tribute to the joining of these two great traditions. A minaret, among the dreaming spires of Oxford, rising beside a quadrangle. Stone drawn from the English villages of Ketton and Clipsham, alongside Malaysian timber for the great auditorium. Every quadrangle here carries a name, and every name carries a debt of gratitude - the King Fahd Quad, the Oman Hall, the Istanbul Courtyard. This is not decoration. It is a physical shukr - a gratitude rendered in stone by many hands and many nations, in acknowledgment of the gift of knowledge that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala has placed within reach of anyone bold enough to seek it.
3. Indeed, I could hardly imagine a more apt setting for the conversation we are here to have today. We have gathered to talk about resilience - how we build it, and how we maintain it - and this building is resilience embodied, raised up from something small and humble: a vision achieved through hard work and persistence. What's more, this building is, as I have mentioned already, a space for bringing together traditions that have not always been in conversation. That is what today is all about.
4. This year's Roundtable is convened around a theme of real consequence for our shared future, the building of resilience at the meeting point of capital, climate, and innovation. These three words are often spoken separately, as though they belong to different conversations held in different rooms. The premise of this Roundtable - and I believe it to be the correct one is that they belong together, and that our future depends upon our ability to unite these three priorities in pursuit of a shared goal.
5. Our world today is replete with dire warnings of the consequences of treating capital and the climate as unrelated concerns. The danger was foretold in an immensely thoughtful work by the late Dr Umer Chapra (d. 2026), titled The Islamic Vision of Development in the Light of Maqasid al-Shariah, published nearly two decades ago.
6. Chapra's argument, distilled, is this. Imam al-Ghazali (d. 1111), the great scholar of the Islamic Golden Age, identified five objectives that the Shariah exists to safeguard. These maqasid are faith, the human self, intellect, posterity, and wealth. Chapra insisted that wealth was never meant to stand alone. It is, in his words, "a trust from God" an amanah. He warned that a civilisation which pursues economic growth while neglecting the other four objectives may enjoy "relatively higher rates of growth" in the short term, but will pay for it in the long run, through inequity, family breakdown, and social unrest.
7. Chapra was writing about human development. He was not, primarily, writing about the state of the planet. And yet his framework naturally extends to it. He reminds us that the environment - "including animals, birds and insects" - is itself a trust, and must be protected, "so that no harm is done to the present or the future generations." Posterity, nasl, was one of his five pillars precisely because no generation is entitled to consume the inheritance of the next.
8. These observations acquire new significance when considered alongside recent events. Here in Oxford, and across Southern and Central Europe this summer, heatwaves have broken temperature records, governments have issued warnings to the elderly to stay indoors, and rivers have run low enough to strand barges. Almost three quarters of the United Kingdom a country, if you'll permit me, notorious for its rain - found itself in drought. And, looking beyond Europe, extreme weather events have claimed far too many lives, with the tragic floods in Nepal coming as the most recent and most devastating episode in a pattern of climate disasters. The environment, that sacred trust, has not been protected; and now Chapra's warning has moved from foresight into lived reality.
9. This escalating emergency is, without question, a consequence of human greed and thoughtlessness. For too long, humanity's purpose, on a global scale, has been growth for growth's sake. Shareholder profits, stock market performance, and GDP: these are what we measure, what we report on, how we judge success and progress. The Quran reminds us that "corruption has flourished on land and sea as a result of people's actions." We were placed upon this earth as its custodians, not its plunderers, and the account now falling due is one that our own conduct has written.
10. Now, I'm not here to pretend that growth isn't important. For a country such as Malaysia, on the path to high-income status, growth is hugely important, for the increased opportunities and broader horizons it brings to our people. But growth as an end in itself - growth driven by greed - this is a problem. Growth alone cannot be our purpose, our driving force as a human race.
11. Instead, we urgently need to bring growth into conversation with the climate emergency. The historic destruction of the environment in pursuit of wealth: that is what has landed us in this crisis. And capital, investment, must now get us out of it. The transition to a resilient and sustainable future cannot be financed by public treasuries alone. The sums required are vast, beyond the reach of any government acting by itself. Private capital, patiently and wisely deployed, must carry a substantial part of this burden. Yet capital, left entirely to its own instincts, tends toward the immediate and the certain. The task before the financial community is therefore to extend its horizons, to learn to price risks that unfold across decades rather than quarters, and to recognize that the returns which matter most in the end are those that endure.
12. This is where, I believe, the principles of Islamic finance can lead the way. A tradition that binds finance to the real economy, insists that capital serve productive and beneficial ends, shares risk rather than shifting it onto others, and forbids the reckless and the harmful this is most well suited to the demands of sustainable investment. We need sukuk structures, waqf-based mechanisms, and green and blue financing instruments that position impact ahead of commercial convenience. We need the courage to challenge attitudes and priorities, rather than fitting our solutions to the status quo: a financial industry that innovates boldly, and prices climate risk honestly modelled on Islamic finance. Indeed, what much of the world has lately begun to call responsible finance, our own tradition has long regarded simply as finance conducted properly.
13. In the context of our conversation today, a key role of responsible investment is, of course, to fund innovation - the third of our three forces. Human ingenuity has repeatedly confounded those who declared a problem to be unsolvable. The technologies of clean energy, efficient agriculture, water management and resilient construction are advancing at a pace that would have seemed improbable only a generation ago. In 2025, wind, solar and other renewables overtook coal as the world's leading source of electricity. For me, this is a sign of progress; and a cause for optimism.
14. Indeed, I firmly believe that research, discovery, and invention have the potential to navigate us through the climate crisis. But intent and motivation matter. According to our tradition, good innovation, bid'ah hasanah, is a tool, and a tool takes its worth from the hand that wields it and the purpose to which it is turned. Consider the story of DDT (Dichloro-Diphenyl-Trichloroethane) - hailed in the mid-twentieth century as the miracle solution to insect-borne disease and crop loss, deployed at extraordinary scale until we discovered it was silently destroying the very ecosystems that sustained the crops it was meant to protect. Take also the more recent temptation of geoengineering - proposals to dim the sun itself with sulphate particles, to buy time, rather than to change course. Each of these innovations is technically ingenious. They also share the same flaw: they treat the symptoms of a mistreated planet, while leaving the disease of unrestrained appetite and growth for growth's sake entirely undisturbed.
15. Instead, what we need is targeted innovation, which is guided by and geared towards behavioural change, as well as technical fixes. Innovation must be underpinned, moreover, by thorough knowledge, hailed in our tradition as a sacred gift as the Quran says, "And He taught Adam the names of all things". When innovation is driven by the right purpose, and founded upon deep understanding, we see real change for the better. Scientific proof that chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) were responsible for the hole in the ozone layer led to global policy change, and as a result, the hole is shrinking. In 2025, the Antarctic ozone hole was the smallest and shortest-lived it had been in five years, confirming for scientists that policies aimed at phasing out ozone-depleting chemicals are having a real and positive impact.
16. Another, similar example is the reduction in acid rain across Europe and North America, which began towards the end of the twentieth century. Once scientists were able to prove that the acidity was caused by emissions of gases like sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, a combination of policy change and technical innovation helped reduce the emissions, which in turn helped reduce acid rainfall. As a result, the affected ecosystems for instance, freshwater lakes are beginning to recover, though acid rain of course remains a pressing issue across much of Asia.
17. From this last example, in particular, I believe there is much we can learn. Firstly, it is a sobering truth that scientific research into the causes of acid rain was initially curbed, and almost prevented altogether, by business interests that viewed the potential impact on their operations as a threat to profits. Influential voices with ulterior motives, protecting their own financial interests over the interests of the natural world: this remains a risk today. I say once again that we must not, we cannot, allow the pursuit of profit to get in the way of the protection of the planet - not least because, in the end, it is a false distinction. Only in the very short term can profit and the planet be considered opposing goals or values. If we fail to reverse the harm we have done to our planet, we will be worse off in all senses of the phrase. The near miss in the case of acid rain research, therefore, stands as a cautionary tale: a reminder to pursue what we know is right for the planet, even in the face of obstruction.
18. The second lesson I would draw from the successful reduction of acid rain is that, sometimes, the true innovation is for us, as humans, to do less. The temptation, in a crisis, is to throw more and more elaborate solutions into the mix - and these can have a valuable impact. But with acid rain, as with the hole in the ozone layer, what we really needed to do, above all else, was reduce our carbon footprint, put less into the environment, not more. With emissions lowered, the lakes whose ecosystems were wiped out by acid rain are gradually recovering on their own. Indeed, our planet's own resilience is nothing short of miraculous.
19. The process of climate recovery will take time. The impact of humanity's mistreatment of the planet did not reveal itself straight away, and the impact of our attempts to undo this damage will take even longer to materialise. We must be patient. We must respect the planet's own healing process. The positive changes we make today could take decades to manifest: and far from being a reason to delay those changes, this is, absolutely, the best reason we have to act now.
20. The Quran describes how, when people are tested - for instance, by a storm at sea - they turn to God with a sincerity that seems unshakeable. We saw this, I think, during the pandemic a brief, global moment of humility, of reflection, of neighbourliness. And we have watched it evaporate just as quickly. A test that is passed and then forgotten has taught us nothing. The measure of a community's faith is not what it does in the storm, but what it does once it reaches the shore.
21. When it comes to the climate emergency, we are, absolutely, in the middle of the storm. And I think there is global - though not unanimous - recognition that we need to act decisively, and act fast. But if we make it to the shore this time, it will not do to simply slip back into old habits, old motivations, and forget this lesson. We need to embed a change of purpose, attitude and behaviour for good. We need to unite the forces of capital and innovation in service of the climate, for a lasting impact and a truly resilient future.
22. Before closing, I want to add a word on justice, for it cannot be absent from this conversation. Those who have contributed least to the warming of our planet are very often those who suffer its consequences most acutely. The nations of the developing world, many of them young, populous, and rich in promise, did not create the greater part of this crisis, yet they stand the most exposed to it. True resilience cannot be built for some while it is denied to others. The capital and the innovation of which we speak must reach those who need them most, and not only those with the means to bear the financial cost.
23. To the young, in particular, I would say this. You will inherit the consequences of the choices made in rooms such as this one, and you are right to hold my generation to account for them. But I urge you to meet this inheritance not with despair, which only paralyses, but with resolve, which builds. Our Prophet sallallahu 'alayhi wassalam taught that even if the Final Hour itself were upon you, and you held a seedling in your hand, you should plant it even then. There is scarcely a wiser counsel from the Prophet for our age. We act, we build, and we plant, because the act itself is right, whatever the outcome may prove to be.
24. My hope for this Roundtable is therefore a practical one. That we leave it resolved to bring the capital we command, the innovation we pursue, and the responsibility we bear into a single and coherent effort. Let us build with the coming generations in mind, and not merely with an eye to the returns of the coming year. And let us remember that the Mother Earth we enjoy is a trust, to be handed on to those who follow us in no worse a condition than we ourselves received it.
25. May Allah grant us wisdom in the stewardship that has been entrusted to us, and make of our efforts a benefit that continues long after we are gone, amin!
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Pedestrian walkways no place for chairs and tables [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: A coalition of residents' associations is gravely disappointed with the government and Kuala Lumpur City Hall (DBKL) over the decision to allow restaurant operators to place tables and chairs on public walkways.
Save Kuala Lumpur (SKL) chairman Datuk M. Ali expressed deep frustration over the lack of public consultation and questioned why authorities are prioritising business operators over the safety and interests of residents.
"Where is the engagement with the people? Where is the minister's engagement with the people on this matter? Why are they so secretive about it?
"They implement and announce it... and let the people suffer. Where is the Madani spirit?" he told the New Sunday Times.
Ali was responding to DBKL's recent move to ease business operations for food premises operators by introducing improvements to streamline services and cut red tape across the federal capital.
This followed recent engagements between Minister in the Prime Minister's Department (Federal Territories) Hannah Yeoh, Kuala Lumpur Mayor Datuk Seri Fadlun Mak Ujud, the Selangor and Kuala Lumpur Chinese Coffee Shop and Tea Shop Owners' Association, and the Malaysia Muslim Restaurant Operators Association.
As part of the initiative, DBKL has given approval for restaurant operators to set up tables and chairs on five-foot walkways with a RM30 monthly permit per table and chair.
Ali said placing  obstacles along pedestrian paths will pose a severe safety hazard to the public.
"They are putting people's lives at great risk. If the place is obstructed, what do I do? I can't wait for them to clear their crowds, so I have to step onto the road.
"When I step onto the road, I am exposed (to vehicles). What safety is City Hall providing us?"
He added that the decision directly contradicted DBKL's long-term urban planning framework, namely the Kuala Lumpur Local Plan 2040.
"This is in contravention of their own city plan. If in the 2040 plan you have identified specific pedestrian passageways, seamlessness and hindrance-free passageways, then why are you making backdoor provisions to create obstacles for pedestrians?"
Ali also blamed the government  for allowing the initiative to move forward without grassroots feedback.
"I hold her (Yeoh) responsible. She should have struck it down and said, 'No, this is a no-go unless the people have expressed their interest or have no objection.'"
He said that the coalition would write officially to Yeoh and Fadlun, demanding an explanation on how the decision was reached.
Ali also called on all residents of Kuala Lumpur to raise their objections against the move.
"The people should object, protest and express concern. Go to the ADU@KL website and keep sending objections that this is not a fair deal. The interest and space of the people must be given due recognition," he said.
The New Sunday Times has reached out to Yeoh and Fadlun over the matter.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: China, Russia, Iran leaders gather in India as BRICS nations seek common ground
Article:
NEW DELHI: Chinese President Xi Jinping joined the leaders of Russia, Iran, India and other BRICS nations in New Delhi on Saturday, seeking common ground on the Middle East war as deep divisions test the 11-member bloc.
Xi told the summit that the Middle East war "does not serve the common interests of the international community", according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua.
Foreign ministers of the BRICS grouping failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May, with Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates divided over the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on February 28.
However, Indian diplomatic sources said leaders were working towards a joint position on some issues as the bloc seeks to bolster its global influence and address conflict, trade turbulence and energy security.
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
"We have to transform this pyramid of privilege into a platform of partnership," Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Xi, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other leaders.
Modi, opening the two-day summit, called for a system "where every country has a voice, every member has a stake, and humanity's development is at the centre of every effort."
He told leaders that BRICS nations "represent 50 perc ent of the world's population, 40 per cent of global GDP, and more than 25 per cent of global trade."
The Middle East conflict was high on the agenda.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
Iran's Pezeshkian attended the summit shortly after warning that the Middle East does not need the United States to be a "regional policeman", with the two countries at war and tensions threatening the vital Strait of Hormuz.
Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is also at the summit in New Delhi, as is Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, and Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan is expected to join later on Saturday.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow's war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.
Modi embraced Putin before talks on Friday. Putin, who last visited India in December 2025, is one of New Delhi's most important strategic partners.
- 'HANDLING DIFFERENCES' -
But the summit's other major focus is China.
Xi's visit is also being closely watched because it is his first to neighbouring India since 2019, and the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the nuclear-armed rivals.
Xi was given a red-carpet welcome, with an honour guard of soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses, and greeted with a handshake by Modi at the summit venue.
His visit comes six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Tibetan border, with ties gradually improving through restored flights, visas and high-level contacts.
Beijing said ahead of his visit that it was "ready to work with India... by strengthening communication, enhancing cooperation, and properly handling differences."
The underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500km high-altitude border with Tibet.
Xi is due to hold face-to-face talks with Modi later on Saturday, according to New Delhi's foreign ministry.
"They are looking for 'early and substantial harvest' when it comes to the border issue," said Pradeep Taneja, a China-India expert at the University of Melbourne.
"You cannot have a build-up of your forces on the border... but at the same time say 'we should continue to have people-to-people relations and economic relationships'."
Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry continuing to complicate ties.
Dozens of Tibetans protested in New Delhi on Friday – exiles, like their Buddhist leader the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959 – waving placards against Xi's visit.--AFP

Title: Asean needs stronger political will, accountability to tackle haze
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR:   The Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution  needs stronger political commitment, faster regional responses and greater accountability if the region is to break the cycle of recurring haze, experts said.
International Islamic University Malaysia political science lecturer Associate Professor Dr Tunku Mohar Tunku Mokhtar said the agreement's main weakness was its reliance on national measures, which could prove ineffective when pollution involved government or government-linked entities.
He said other mechanisms, including joint emergency responses and regional coordination, had also yet to produce   results.
Previously, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said the Asean mechanism on transboundary haze had room for improvement, as smoke from forest fires in Indonesia continued to affect Malaysia.
He said Asean ministers should  review the  mechanism given the impact of transboundary haze on public health.
Tunku Mohar said  Asean's consensus-based decision-making could make  reforms difficult.
"In the end, member states will end up with rhetoric of unity."
He also pointed to a lack of political will among member states, which  had contributed to perceptions that governments could be complicit in allowing the  problem to persist.
Asean's principle of non-interference was another hurdle, he said, although addressing a cross-border environmental problem should not be viewed as an infringement of national sovereignty.
"In some common issues such as  transboundary haze, a call for a regional solution should not be understood as an attack on another state's sovereignty."
He said Asean  needed to develop a stronger regional understanding that a clean environment was a basic human right and that addressing haze was a shared responsibility.
"If the cause of haze is natural, then affected members must allow other Asean members to assist in solving it.
"If it is caused by human activities, they should be stopped and  punished."
Universiti Teknologi Mara  senior   political science lecturer Shahidah Abdul Razak said Asean should place greater emphasis on early intervention.
She said member states should respond more quickly when hotspots were detected, with faster information-sharing, clearer identification of fire sources and closer coordination between relevant agencies.
She said the recurring problem was driven by a combination of economic interests, land-clearing practices, enforcement challenges and weather conditions.
"Burning is still one of the cheaper ways to clear land, and during prolonged dry weather, fires can spread very quickly, especially on peatland.
"We have become better at detecting hotspots, but detecting a fire and preventing it from happening are two different things.
"When smoke crosses borders and affects people in neighbouring countries, it is no longer  a domestic issue."
Shahidah said Asean needed to ensure that information gathered through its regional mechanisms translated into concrete action, including identifying those responsible for fires and establishing greater transparency around land ownership and control.
"At the end of the day, progress should not only be measured by how many meetings Asean holds, but whether we  see fewer fires and  haze episodes," she said.

Title: BRICS nations call for 'maximum restraint' in Middle East war
Article:
NEW DELHI: Members of the 11-nation BRICS group including China, Russia, Iran and India called for calm in the Middle East at a summit in New Delhi on Saturday, overcoming earlier divisions to issue a joint statement.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, who joined Russian, Iranian, Indian and other leaders in India's capital, told the summit that the Middle East war "does not serve the common interests of the international community."
Foreign ministers of the BRICS grouping had failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May, with Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates divided over the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Feb 28.
But leaders issued a statement on Saturday after intense diplomatic efforts by host India, as the bloc seeks to bolster its global influence and address conflict, trade turbulence and energy security.
"We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in Middle East/West Asia," the joint statement said, adding the countries "call for exercising maximum restraint, as well as avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation."
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
"We have to transform this pyramid of privilege into a platform of partnership," Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Xi, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other leaders as he opened the two-day summit.
Modi said BRICS nations "represent 50 per cent of the world's population, 40 per cent of global GDP and more than 25 per cent of global trade."
But finding balance in the bloc is a tough diplomatic task.
India maintains cordial relations with both Iran and US ally Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
Iran's Pezeshkian attended the summit shortly after warning that the Middle East does not need the United States to be a "regional policeman", with the two countries at war and tensions threatening the vital Strait of Hormuz.
Pezeshkian met with Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on the summit sidelines.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow's war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.
Modi embraced Putin before talks on Friday. The Russian president, who last visited India in December 2025, is one of New Delhi's most important strategic partners.
- 'HANDLING DIFFERENCES' -
Xi's participation is also being closely watched because it is his first visit to neighbouring India since 2019, and the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the nuclear-armed rivals.
Xi was given a red-carpet welcome, with an honour guard of soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses.
"Although our two countries are different in many respects, they are fully capable of complementing each other's strengths, supporting one another, achieving mutual success and advancing together," Xi said as he met Modi, in a video released from New Delhi.
His visit comes six years after a deadly military clash along the disputed Tibetan border between China and India, with ties gradually improving through restored flights, visas and high-level contacts.
The underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500km high-altitude border.
India's foreign ministry said in a statement after the meeting that "the two leaders expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question."
Modi "underlined the need for both sides to observe existing agreements and understandings on border related issues," the foreign ministry added.
Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry continuing to complicate ties.
"Both sides should... work hand-in-hand to promote high-quality major financial cooperation, advocate an equal and sustainable global order, and foster an economic globalisation that is open and inclusive," Xi said.
Dozens of Tibetans protested in New Delhi on Friday – exiles, like their Buddhist leader the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959 – waving placards against Xi's visit.--AFP

Title: Modi, Xi push business links, border peace as India-China ties revive
Article:
NEW DELHI: India and China's leaders pledged on Saturday to build up business and transport links, New Delhi said, as both rebuild ties badly damaged by a 2020 military clash on their disputed Himalayan border.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping met on the sidelines of a summit of the BRICS group of emerging nations in New Delhi — Xi's first trip to India in seven years.
Military tensions have eased, but businesses in both countries say they continue to face hurdles, including red tape, visa delays and restrictions on selling industrial equipment.
"The two leaders ... underscored the need to further promote cultural exchanges, business linkages and greater mobility between the two countries," the Indian foreign ministry said in a statement.
"On economic and trade relations, they underlined the need to address each other's concerns, including structural trade imbalance and supply chain issues, and facilitation of meaningful and predictable market access," it said.
Bilateral trade reached a record US$155.6 billion in 2025, according to Chinese customs data.
China has become India's largest source of imports, with Indian purchases from China rising to about US$132 billion in the 2025/26 fiscal year. India's exports to China remain much smaller, leaving New Delhi with a trade deficit of more than US$100 billion.
Xi said China has always viewed and developed China-India relations from a strategic and long-term perspective, state-run Xinhua news agency reported.
Institutional exchanges between the two countries are gradually being restored, the list of areas for cooperation is growing and bilateral trade has reached a new high, Xi said according to Xinhua.
China and India fought a brief but brutal border war in 1962, and their relationship soured again after the 2020 border skirmish killed 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers.
Ties began recovering at the end of 2024 after Xi and Modi agreed to end their military stand-off in the western Himalayas.
Irritants remain as both countries continue to maintain substantial military deployments in the Himalayas and border talks make slow progress.
Modi said that peace in the border areas remained an essential basis for the continued development of bilateral relations, according to the Indian statement.
The nuclear-armed neighbours share a roughly 3,800km, largely unmarkedfrontier.--REUTERS

Title: Trump backs Irish unification, calls it 'a fantastic thing'
Article:
DOONBEG, Ireland: Donald Trump said Saturday he would "love to see" a united Ireland, wading into a politically sensitive subject as he embarked on a two-day Irish visit that blurs the lines between his presidency and personal business interests.
After meeting Ireland's Prime Minister Micheal Martin in Dublin, Trump said reunification of the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland – split for over a century – would be "a fantastic thing."
"It's going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now," he told reporters, adding "the UK will have something to say about it, obviously."
The island of Ireland has been split between the Irish republic in the south and Northern Ireland, which is part of the United Kingdom, since 1921.
Under the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, which ended three decades of sectarian violence in Northern Ireland that killed about 3,000 people, a referendum can be held if the UK government determines a majority there is likely to favour joining the Republic of Ireland.
Republic of Ireland voters would also have to endorse reunification in a poll for it to happen.
The United States has previously adopted a neutral position on the issue.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham insisted last month that a unity referendum was "off the table", drawing a sharp response from the pro-unity party Sinn Fein.
Asked about Trump's comments, a spokesperson for his Downing Street office referred reporters to comments Burnham made in parliament Wednesday when he vowed to "stick to the Good Friday Agreement 100 per cent."
However Gavin Robinson, leader of the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party, said on X that "as unionists we are not interested in the destruction of our country by joining with the Irish Republic."
- DIVERGENCES -
Trump had touched down at Dublin airport shortly before 8.25am (0725 GMT) under a security operation dubbed one of the largest ever mounted in Ireland and reportedly costing 20 million euros (US$23 million).
At least 4,000 police and other personnel, including snipers, have been mobilised.
In Dublin, at least 2,000 protesters waving Palestinian flags and holding placards rallied Saturday lunchtime against the president's visit, chanting "Donald Trump's not welcome here", AFP reporters saw.
One sign read "no imperialists in Ireland" while some held explicit inflatable balloons showing Trump in sex acts with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Trump is a warmonger," student Cillian Whelan, 19, told AFP. "He has no right to be in my country. He should be on trial."
One small group of demonstrators – dressed in black and wearing masks and dark glasses – set a US flag on fire, according to The Irish Times.
Smaller protests also occurred at Shannon Airport, where the US leader transited, and in Doonbeg on Ireland's west coast, where the Trump Organization's 2014-purchased course is hosting golf's Irish Open tournament.
Police said three women – aged in their 20s, 30s and 40s – had appeared in a western Irish court late Saturday after being arrested for separate trespass and public order offences there.
After completing engagements in Dublin, Trump made a dramatic landing in Doonbeg aboard Marine One, and was soon photographed watching over the 18th green during the third round of the Open flanked by his sons Don Jr. and Eric.
He was reportedly given a rapturous reception during a brief appearance in the resort's members' bar, with drinkers chanting "USA."
- 'STRONG VIEW' -
Earlier in Dublin, Trump appeared to receive a frostier reception from left-wing President Catherine Connolly, an outspoken critic of the US leader.
"I conveyed the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted," Connolly said in a post-meeting statement.
He then met Martin, when the Iran war and US tariffs on EU pharmaceuticals and immigration were on the agenda.
Ireland and the United States have long been close allies, partly because of their common ancestral ties.
But the Irish government's politics diverge sharply from those of the Trump administration on many issues, with Ireland being one of Europe's most pro-Palestinian countries.
It is among several countries, including Spain, the UK and France, that have announced a trade ban targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
In Doonbeg, some 40,000 fans are expected at the Open over the weekend. Trump may even award the trophy Sunday.
The 80-year-old golf-mad president has promoted his family's courses and other businesses unabashedly since returning to the White House for his second presidential stint in January 2025.
Trinity College Dublin US history professor Daniel Gear told AFP that Trump "sees little difference between his private interests and his role as president."--AFP

Title: #NSTviral: DBKL urged to act on double-parking gridlock along Jalan Pudu Lama
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Kuala Lumpur City Hall (DBKL) has been urged to take action against illegal parking along Jalan Pudu Lama, where double-parking has reportedly reduced the two-way road to a single congested lane.
The issue was highlighted in a viral post on Threads by user @zebra.animal.53, who tagged DBKL's parking enforcement account and questioned the lack of action over vehicles parked on both sides of the road.
"Can DBKL actually do something here? From Bursa Malaysia to Jalan Pudu Lama, cars are parked on both sides of the road even though it is a two-way street," the user posted after tagging DBKL parking on Threads.
The netizen highlighted how indiscriminate double-parking eliminates space for vehicles to safely pass or manoeuvre, leaving drivers stranded in standoffs when vehicles travelling in opposite directions met.
"If there are no cars behind, you can still reverse to make way. But what happens if neither side wants to yield?" the user said.
The post drew responses from other users, with one, @mr.allent, claiming DBKL had been lax in enforcing parking regulations in the area.
Another user, @tgrosmi, suggested that proper parking bays or a designated no-parking area be introduced to prevent traffic congestion.

Title: Former judge Syed Ahmad Idid denies requesting RM10.5mil compensation over 1996 resignation
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Former High Court judge Datuk Syed Ahmad Idid Syed Abdullah Idid has clarified that he never requested, demanded, or set a compensation amount of RM10.5 million from the Malaysian government over his resignation nearly 30 years ago.
He clarified to clear up confusion regarding the reported claim through a letter sent today to Malaysian Bar president Anand Raj.
Syed Ahmad Idid also expressed his deep appreciation to the Malaysian Bar for its firm stance in defending the independence and integrity of the judiciary through its statement issued yesterday, titled "The Judiciary Must Be, and Remain, Steadfast in Upholding the Rule of Law and Incorruptible".
He explained that the RM10.5 million figure linked to him in recent reports actually referred to other judges affected by the 1988 judicial crisis.
"Those circumstances were materially different from my case. Therefore, I consider it inappropriate for my case to be equated with theirs based on that figure," he said.
"On my part, I have never requested, demanded, or specified an amount of RM10.5 million, nor have I suggested any specific sum as compensation from the government," he added.
Elaborating further, he emphasised that his resignation was not merely a personal matter involving pensions or financial compensation, but a fundamental question of legal and constitutional principles regarding how a High Court judge resigns.
"My intention and priority have always transcended personal interest. An independent judiciary relies on judges who can execute their constitutional duties with complete integrity without fear or favour," he said.
"Anyone who raises truth-based concerns regarding misconduct within our institutions should not be punished, but protected," he added.
He expressed hope that his experiences three decades ago would help strengthen the judicial institution for future generations.
Syed Ahmad Idid resigned as a High Court judge in 1996 after exposing alleged misconduct and corruption within the judiciary through an anonymous letter containing 112 allegations against certain judges at the time.

Title: BRICS calls for immediate restoration of WTO dispute settlement mechanism
Article:
NEW DELHI: BRICS has called for the immediate restoration of an accessible, effective, and fully functioning two-tier binding World Trade Organisation (WTO) dispute settlement mechanism while reaffirming its support for a rules-based multilateral trading system.
"We remain committed to active engagement in multilateral negotiations in Geneva, especially in the debates regarding the reform of the WTO," the grouping said in a 45-page declaration released today.
BRICS said it would enhance coordination under its Informal Consultative Framework to address challenges undermining the WTO's effectiveness and credibility.
The grouping also called for the appointment of new Appellate Body members without delay, stressing the importance of strengthening the organisation's authority, effectiveness, inclusiveness, and relevance.
"We strongly advocate for the immediate restoration of an accessible, effective, fully functioning, two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism as a foundation for trust and predictability for all WTO members, and the appointment of new Appellate Body members without further delay," the declaration stated.
The grouping expressed serious concern over the proliferation of unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures inconsistent with WTO rules, warning that such actions threaten to reduce global trade, disrupt supply chains, and deepen economic disparities. It also condemned unilateral coercive measures contrary to international law, including economic and secondary sanctions not authorised by the United Nations Security Council.
Furthermore, BRICS encouraged the New Development Bank (NDB) to expand its capacity to mobilise resources, foster innovation, expand local currency financing, diversify funding sources, and support impactful projects advancing sustainable development.
"We recognise NDB as a crucial BRICS institution for promoting sustainable development, reducing inequalities and supporting resilience in emerging economies," it said.
Echoing the aspirations of the Global South to integrate into the multilateral trading system, BRICS supported Ethiopia and Iran's bids to join the WTO, while acknowledging China's expansion of zero-tariff treatment to 53 African nations with which it maintains diplomatic ties.
China is set to assume the BRICS chairmanship in 2027 and host the 19th BRICS Leaders' Summit.
Initially established by Brazil, Russia, India, and China, the forum expanded to include South Africa in 2011, followed by Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates in 2023, and Indonesia in 2024.
Malaysia, alongside Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Nigeria, Thailand, Vietnam, Uganda, and Uzbekistan, joined as BRICS partner countries.
India, which previously held the chairmanship in 2012, 2016, and 2021, assumed its fourth BRICS chairmanship on Jan 1, 2026, marking 20 years since the grouping's establishment.

Title: Dr L. Sivanaesan appointed new MMA president
Article:
IPOH: Dr L Sivanaesan has been appointed the new president of the Malaysian Medical Association (MMA), succeeding Datuk Dr R Thirunavukarasu, whose term ended today.
The former MMA president-elect previously served as chairman of MMA Selangor, honorary deputy secretary of the association for two terms, and chairman of the MMA Private Practitioners Section from 2023 to 2024.
Speaking at the MMA 2026 dinner here tonight, Sivanaesan said retaining doctors in Malaysia's public healthcare system will be his priority as the nation faces growing healthcare demands and an increasing need for medical personnel.
"Training a doctor takes many years and requires significant investment," he said. "When experienced doctors leave the public system, we do not simply lose a member of the workforce; we lose experience, expertise and the continuity of care they provide to patients."
Sivanaesan said retaining doctors cannot be addressed simply by increasing the number of medical graduates, noting that greater attention must be given to doctors' career progression, working environment, professional development and long-term prospects within the public healthcare system.

Title: Man arrested over robbery and assault of two Rohingya men
Article:
JOHOR BARU: Police have arrested a 25-year-old local man suspected of robbing, assaulting, and threatening two Rohingya men in Taman Perling.
Johor police chief Datuk Ab Rahaman Arsad said police received reports regarding the incidents on Sept 9 and 10 from the victims, aged 25 and 35.
"The first victim was riding a motorcycle looking for lawn-mowing clients when the suspect stopped him, demanding and snatching his UNHCR card and lawnmower.
"The suspect then confronted the second victim nearby, demanding his UNHCR card before punching and threatening him during an altercation," Ab Rahaman said in a statement today.
Following a tip-off, a team from the Johor Baru Utara district police headquarters criminal investigation department arrested the suspect in Taman Perling at 5.40pm yesterday.
Ab Rahaman said police seized a lawnmower, a parang, a UNHCR card, a motorcycle key, and a set of clothes.
The suspect, who tested negative for drugs but has a prior criminal record, has been remanded for seven days until Sept 18 to assist investigations.
"Police are verifying the authenticity of the victims' UNHCR cards with the UNHCR Office in Kuala Lumpur. At the same time, we stress that any party other than the authorities who detains, blocks, or checks an individual's identification documents is acting against the law," he said.
The case is being investigated under Section 392 of the Penal Code for robbery, Section 323 for voluntarily causing hurt, and Section 506 for criminal intimidation.

Title: Johari, Piyush Goyal discuss stronger Malaysia-India economic ties
Article:
NEW DELHI: Investment, trade and economic cooperation between Malaysia and India were the focus of a bilateral meeting between Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani and India's Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal during Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim's visit to New Delhi.

Title: Could AI really kill us all?
Article:
STARK warnings from artificial intelligence researchers that advanced forms of the technology could wipe out humanity have raised questions over whether governments are moving fast enough to regulate it.
What are the potential dangers of "superintelligent" computer systems, and should we be worried?
AI experts have long described the threat as critical.
In 2023, hundreds of AI scientists and industry figures, including the heads of top   US labs, signed a "statement on AI extinction risk" calling for the issue to be treated as seriously as pandemics or nuclear war.
If an out-of-control future AI deems that humans are obstructing its goals, it could use robots to "synthesise and spread novel pathogens", said Stuart Russell, computer science professor at the University of California, Berkeley.
Or it could "convince people to initiate nuclear war, including by hacking into early warning systems", Russell, a prominent voice on AI safety, said.
Such existential fears do not concern current AI systems, he said. But as the technology improves, it could take lethal action beyond our understanding, such as by removing oxygen from the atmosphere.
"We are less intelligent than superintelligent AI. If you ask chimpanzees how humans could wipe them out, they probably wouldn't be able to give you all the right answers."
In the meantime, "in the next year or two, I think the risk is higher from human misuse", Russell added, such as an AI-enabled terror attack.
"The stakes are well-understood," Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old researcher, wrote on X  last week, announcing his resignation from US AI startup Anthropic.
"But they are locked in a race to get there first," he added, saying that Anthropic "believes no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves".
Anthropic this year removed a pledge from its safety charter to halt development of its models if it failed to control their risks.
It argued that if it unilaterally paused its work, its less cautious rivals would dominate the industry, making it less safe overall.
"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," said Coxon, who previously worked at ChatGPT maker Open-AI.
He accused both companies of "gambling with our lives" as they strive to develop AI models capable of self-improvement.
Fears are heightened over rogue AI after OpenAI technology operating outside human supervision hacked into Hugging Face, a repository of AI models.
"We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!" Anthropic safety executive Evan Hubinger chimed in on X, estimating the risk at more than 10 per cent over the next decade.
It's important to remember that doom-laden percentage predictions are "absolutely unscientific", said Hussein Abbass, a computing professor at UNSW Canberra.
"The situation is still controllable, and it can be managed," Abbass said.
But governments should not sit on their hands when it comes to regulating AI, he added, urging an "agile" approach as AI development accelerates.
Both Anthropic and OpenAI are expected to go public soon, and some sceptics say scary warnings make AI appear powerful and worthy of large investments.
Others argue that focusing on the risk of extinction distracts from more pressing problems caused by AI, from job losses to machines discriminating against minorities.
In July, more than 1,000 tech employees, including Anthropic's CEO, called on Washington to support a coordinated slowdown in the development of the most advanced AI systems.
OpenAI halted training of its latest models for two weeks in August before resuming it under tighter controls.
The United States has been firmly against global regulation of the sector that could stifle innovation.
But the  hacking capabilities of the most cutting-edge models have given Washington pause, with recent Anthropic and OpenAI releases delayed over national security concerns.
Even then, "we don't want to restrict them where all of a sudden we come in second to China", President Donald Trump has said.
"Maybe it will take a massive, Chernobyl-scale disaster to get governments to act," Russell said, urging them to establish a licensing regime for AI, as exists with aviation, medicine or water supply.
"Perhaps at some point governments will remember that their voters prefer not to be dead."
* The writer is from AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: The morning that changed everything
Article:
TWENTY-SIX years ago, a journalist with about six years of experience decided he needed to further his studies to get a degree to improve his chances of growing in the industry.
He chose a university well known for its mass communications courses — and one that was affordable — in a Midwestern part of the United States.
The next year, he was appointed news editor of the university's newspaper due in large part to his experience, meagre as it was.
One fateful morning that year, the journalist in question woke up a little late and rushed to get ready, forgoing his usual habit of watching the news  on TV.
As he got into the elevator of his dormitory later, he heard some others talking about an aircraft crashing into the Twin Towers in New York.
The journalist thought nothing of it, thinking it was  a     light aircraft.
He did not realise then the scale of  what was happening on Sept 11, 2001.
It was only when he got to his first class of the day — in a remarkable coincidence, it was on terrorism — that he knew exactly what was going on.
A TV had been wheeled into the classroom, and students were watching as things unfolded.
But the students actually knew what was happening before it unfolded on TV.
The lecturer was a retired
lieutenant-colonel in the US Air Force who had once been posted at the US embassy in Moscow. She had many friends in the intelligence agencies and stepped out constantly to answer or make phone calls.
She kept her students informed, telling them about the crash into the Pentagon and the fourth aircraft, even before it crashed in Pennsylvania.
We all know the story of what unfolded that day. The chaos, the weeping, the fear, the death, the anger. The first thing that hit everyone, however, was  shock and disbelief.
In the university's theatre, which holds about 700 people, more than 1,000 students and lecturers sat and stood in shock, watching a large screen showing a news channel.
Then, as the first tower came crashing down, a collective gasp rocked the theatre. This was followed by the exact opposite — complete and utter silence, a deafening silence broken only  by the sounds of sobbing.
The university cancelled classes for the rest of the day and warned foreign students to stay at home.
The journalist received calls from worried friends telling him to stay home and not attend a vigil being planned for that night. He had to ignore their advice, though, as he had a job to do.
That worry came to nothing, as everyone was supportive of foreign students and looked out for them.
The fears were justified, but proved  unnecessary. There was only sorrow that lingered.
Twenty-five years on, the journalist still remembers everything that happened that day as if it were a mere 25 minutes ago.
Every thought, every emotion — fear, sadness, anger — still lingers.
Sept 11, 2001, will remain with him all the days of his life. It is there alongside the memories of  Malaysia Airlines flights MH370 and MH17.
The people who died that day will remain a part of his memory, despite the fact that he did not know them. But so will all those who showed their concern for him.
It is at our worst times that people come through for us. Let us all, in others' times of need, be there for them.

Title: NST Leader: Greater Sabah, Sarawak representation a step towards equity
Article:
THIS marks a positive and long-awaited step towards addressing the imbalance in Malaysia's federal structure and fulfilling the broader spirit of the Malaysia Agreement 1963 (MA63). There is no disagreement here.
Greater representation for Sabah and Sarawak is a positive recognition that Malaysia's federal structure must evolve to reflect the realities and aspirations of all its regions. It is a evolution, not a revolution. But the goal should not be to create winners and losers between East and West Malaysia.
A stronger voice for Sabah and Sarawak should be seen as strengthening the entire federation.
The real test will be whether the increased representation leads to better policies, greater development and a more equitable partnership within Malaysia. This is one more step towards that direction.
Greater representation would recognise the special position of Sabah and Sarawak as partners in the formation of Malaysia. This would signal better representation for remote communities.
Constituencies in Sabah and Sarawak can be geographically vast and difficult to serve. More representatives could help bring Parliament closer to remote communities. It could lead to a more balanced federation: national policies should reflect the needs and perspectives of all regions.
A stronger Borneo voice can enrich national debate and improve policymaking.
However, representation must mean more than numbers. More members of parliament alone will not solve Sabah  and Sarawak's long-standing concerns over infrastructure, healthcare, education and development. Greater representation must be accompanied by real progress.
Hectares of forests are gone over the years, yet very little evidence of economic development shows up. Don't get us wrong.
There were, of course, spurts of it in the 1970s, 1980s and more evidently, in the late 2000s. Spurt doesn't do development justice. Developed years, they called them.
There is a peculiar connection between politics and economics. If political leadership is strong, it will drive development like it does now in Sarawak.
One won't be wrong to say that Kuching has seen a sea change in the last decade or two. Likewise, 20 years of commerce  is a great persuader too. At times, it is otherwise.
In Sabah, it is quieter. Now, with more Borneo voices in Parliament, Kuala Lumpur gets louder — as long as equity is somewhere there. "No one must be left behind" is a great line, if it just remains a line in a prime minister's keynote address at an international forum.
Yes, equity is the point. In the beginning is the end.

Title: Sarawak extends school closures in Serian, Lubok Antu over haze
Article:
KUCHING: The state education department has extended the temporary closure of schools in the Serian and Lubok Antu districts until the Air Pollutant Index (API) reading drops below 200.
The Sarawak State Education Department said the decision followed continuous monitoring of API readings via the Department of Environment's Malaysian Air Pollutant Index Management System (APIMS) and reports from the Malaysian Meteorological Department.
However, all primary and secondary schools under 12 District Education Offices —  Kuching, Padawan, Bau, Lundu, Samarahan, Simunjan, Sri Aman, Kanowit, Julau, Meradong, Bintulu, and Tatau/Sebauh—will operate as usual starting Monday.
"Any changes regarding school operations or latest developments will be announced from time to time," the department said in a statement tonight.
The department added that the Education Ministry, in collaboration with the National Disaster Management Agency (Nadma), will soon distribute face masks to students, teachers, and staff at schools in severely affected areas.
The department reiterated that the welfare, health, and safety of students remain its top priority, especially during hot or hazy weather.
"If the API reading exceeds 100, all outdoor activities involving students must be halted. When the API reading exceeds 200, all schools in the affected area or district must close immediately. If the reading exceeds 500, teachers and school staff are not required to report for duty," it said, adding that schools will reopen once the API falls below 200.
Parents and guardians concerned about their children's health may keep them at home, provided they inform the school. Temporary closures may also be ordered based on recommendations from the Sarawak State Disaster Management Committee.
The department reminded all district education offices and schools to take preventive measures, including ensuring an adequate supply of clean drinking water, encouraging students to bring their own water, and advising them to wear face masks and hydrate frequently to regulate body temperature.

Title: Sanusi, Mahdzir set to meet over possible Pas-Umno cooperation
Article:
SUNGAI PETANI: A meeting between Kedah Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Muhammad Sanusi Md Nor and state Umno leaders is being arranged to discuss possible cooperation between the two parties.
Sanusi, who is also Kedah Pas deputy commissioner, said he had been informed about the proposed meeting and his office was arranging a suitable date.
"I have also obtained Kedah Pas' approval to hold an initial meeting with former Kedah Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Mahdzir Khalid from Umno. I was told he wants to come with Datuk Seri Ahmad Bashah Md Hanipah.
"We have asked the office to arrange a suitable time. I had to seek Kedah Pas' approval first. I am not the party chief in Kedah; I am the second-in-command. I have a leader. Kedah Pas has also agreed to the initial meeting," he told reporters after officiating the 2026 Sungai Petani Municipal Council Sepak Raga Tuju Carnival here today.
Mahdzir, who is Kedah Umno liaison chairman, had previously expressed his intention to meet Muhammad Sanusi to discuss possible cooperation between Umno and Pas in the state.
He had said the meeting would be arranged after the conclusion of the 2026 Umno General Assembly.
Sanusi said the initial meeting was important to understand what Umno wanted to discuss before any further negotiations were held.
"Maybe they want to ask about seats. I understand the status quo is being maintained.
"If Umno-BN does not have any more seats, we can explore which seats they want to contest. I am not sure; perhaps that is what they want to discuss. I am just mentioning it for now," he said.
On seat negotiations, he said any discussions should not be based solely on the political situation in a particular state, but must take into account the overall national picture.
He said this would allow adjustments to be made between states based on negotiations at the central level.
"Negotiations in Melaka, for example, cannot be conducted at the state level alone. They must take the whole country into account.
"If we discuss only within the state, it will be difficult to shift things around. It is the same in Kedah, Kelantan and Terengganu, where it is difficult to make adjustments.
"So, other states must also be taken into account. Whatever decision is made by the central leadership will be conveyed to the states, and I will abide by it.
"For now, it is only an initial meeting. We will see what they want to discuss. I do not have any idea yet. That is all," he said.
